item.title: Failures of Digitalization in the Workplace
item.content:encoded:
Heiner Heiland, University of Göttingen

Annemarie Kern, University of Göttingen

Sarah Nies, University of Göttingen

Samuel Rieger, University of Göttingen

Matthias Sommer, University of Göttingen

This special issue examines widespread failures of digital technologies in the workplace, challenging narratives that treat digitalization as a solution to organizational challenges. Despite promises of improved efficiency and work conditions, major systems failures, abandoned IT projects, and everyday workplace malfunctions are common. The issue argues that examining these failures reveals fundamental contradictions in how digital technologies are designed and implemented within work organizations.

Research on digitalization failures remains sparse in labor studies despite their ubiquity in workplaces, with most attention directed toward technical aspects rather than the intersection of work processes and technology. This special issue seeks contributions analyzing failure as a systematic phenomenon embedded in operational contexts, power relations, and conflicting interests—not merely as technical malfunctions but as windows into structural contradictions in work organization.

Appel publié par New Technology Work and Employment. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Theoretical examination of failure in digital work processes, including concepts of technical rationality, solutionism, and sociological perspectives on inscription and closure
  • Empirical investigation of processes and consequences of failure in digitized work, service, and production processes
  • The role of technological expectations and promises in digital transformations and their relationship to actual outcomes
  • Conflicts of interest and class dynamics in digitalization and their influence on success and failure
  • Standards and measures of success for digital processes and attribution of failure
  • Management and negotiation of digital technology failures within work processes
  • Contradictions between technological promises and actual effects on work

Timeline

  • April 30, 2027: Submission deadline

item.title: Platformisation as an Organising Logic of Inequality
item.content:encoded:
Amanda Peticca-Harris, Grenoble Ecole de Management

Annalisa Murgia, University of Milan

Julieta Haidar, Workers' Innovation Centre-CONICET

This special issue examines how digital platforms function as systems that organise and reinforce inequality rather than simply producing it as an outcome. Platform labour operates as survival work for those already positioned within broader structures of inequality, including migrants, workers excluded from formal employment, and women managing care responsibilities. The issue seeks work that connects domains often treated separately—such as legal status, gender, and labour stratification—and explores how these intersect in shaping platform participation across geographical contexts.

Contributors are encouraged to examine how livelihoods are assembled through platformisation across labour, migration, and everyday life, with particular attention to care work and social reproduction. The issue also welcomes research on how workers navigate, adapt to, and contest platform-mediated inequalities through resistance, collective organising, and everyday survival strategies, recognising that agency emerges within the systems that organise inequality itself.

Appel publié par New Technology Work and Employment. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • To what extent do platform-based systems depend on inequality? How do they organise it?
  • In what ways are insecurity and risk embedded within platform-based systems?
  • How is labour supply structured through marginalised populations within platform economies?
  • How are visibility, ratings, access to work, and valuation differentially organised across workers and contexts?
  • How are platform systems becoming embedded across domains such as mobility, food, care, logistics, and urban life?
  • In what ways do platform arrangements rely on, reproduce, and organise gendered, racialised, classed, generational, ableist, or otherwise undervalued forms of labour?
  • How are livelihoods assembled through platform work across contexts shaped by migration, informality, and low incomes?
  • How do workers combine multiple income streams, care responsibilities, and relational resources to sustain everyday life?
  • What forms of agency, everyday tactics, informal solidarities, survival strategies, resistance, or adaptation emerge in response to inequalities embedded within platform-based systems?
  • What methodological approaches can make visible the unequal, relational, embodied, and infrastructural dimensions of platform-mediated work and livelihood?

Timeline

  • May 31, 2027: Full-length paper submission deadline

item.title: The Algorithmic Turn: AI, Professional Labour, and the Reconfiguration of Work
item.content:encoded:
Caroline Barrett, University of York

Lutfun Nahar Lata, Murdoch University

Daniel Muzio, University of York

François Schoenberger, University of Oxford

This special issue examines how artificial intelligence and algorithmic management are reshaping professional work, situating current technological changes within a longer historical context of technological reconfiguration. It investigates whether AI threatens professional expertise by making knowledge more accessible or whether expertise remains fundamentally relational and generated through human interactions.

The call explores how power may shift as new AI-focused occupations emerge while established professions face disruption from new entrants and business models. Within professional service firms, hierarchical structures may flatten as AI reduces demand for junior professionals. The collection also addresses how these transformations impact individual professionals' identities, agency, and the ethical questions arising in AI-integrated practice.

Drawing on momentum from a successful conference stream, this open call welcomes global research spanning healthcare, creative labour, knowledge services, higher education, and the professions of those who build AI systems themselves.

Appel publié par New Technology Work and Employment. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How AI displaces or enhances professional work; implications of AI-driven knowledge accessibility for occupational closure; erosion or evolution of professions as exclusive knowledge domains
  • New business models challenging traditional regulation; AI's impact on hierarchies, leverage ratios, and power dynamics; role of legacy institutions in mediating change; new forms of organizational experimentation
  • Shifting lived experiences, identities, and agency of individual professionals; emerging essential skills such as digital literacy and ethical reasoning; new ethical challenges; adaptation of professional training; forms of resistance or compliance to algorithmic oversight
  • The rise or decline of specific occupations due to AI; potential resurgence of manual and craft labour; how professionals are shaping the future of their fields; emerging alternative models of professionalism
  • Healthcare and diagnostic expertise, particularly AI implementation in medical imaging, digital documentation, and radiology
  • Algorithmic transformations and emerging collective agency among journalists, visual media freelancers, and creative workers
  • Disruption or transition of traditional expertise across legal sectors, translation platforms, and academic institutions
  • How data scientists, ML engineers, computer programmers, and data analysts find their own elite expertise reconfigured by AI systems they build
  • Shifting lived experiences, professional identities, and relational reinforcement of client expertise in modern institutional settings
